front_old: Evaluate the effects of unemployment, and the significance of migration and skills.
back_old:
• Individuals — lower incomes and living standards, skills erode, health suffers.
  • Government and society — lower tax revenue and higher welfare spending widen the deficit; social costs rise.
  • Firms — weaker sales, though a larger labour pool can lower hiring costs.

Migration cuts unemployment where migrants fill shortages, and migrants' spending creates jobs; competition can raise unemployment in particular low-skilled sectors.

Skills determine who escapes structural unemployment.

front_old: Evaluate the limitations of GDP for comparing living standards, and the national happiness evidence.
back_old:
• GDP per capita masks inequality.
  • It excludes unpaid work, leisure and environmental quality.
  • It counts welfare-reducing 'bads' like pollution clean-up.
  • It struggles with quality improvements.
  • It misses the informal economy.

Hence the interest in national wellbeing: the UK measures subjective happiness alongside GDP, and rising real incomes raise reported happiness only weakly beyond a point.

front_old: What causes a current account deficit, and how does correcting one conflict with other objectives?
back_old:
Causes:

  • High consumer spending and low saving pulling in imports.
  • Weak competitiveness and low productivity.
  • A strong currency.
  • Slowdown in export markets.
  • Structural issues such as deindustrialisation.

Corrections trade off against other objectives — cutting demand through fiscal or monetary tightening slows growth and raises unemployment; supply-side improvement works but slowly and at a cost.

Economies are interconnected through trade, so one country's deficit is another's surplus.

front_old: Define the current account of the balance of payments, and name the remaining indicator.
back_old:
The balance of payments records all transactions between a country and the rest of the world; the current account is the part that records trade in goods and services, income flows, and current transfers.

The final indicator is productivity — output per worker (or per hour worked) — which drives long-run growth and competitiveness.

front_old: Distinguish the types of public expenditure, and why governments levy taxes.
back_old:
• Current expenditure — day-to-day spending on public-sector wages and consumables (teachers' pay, medicines).
  • Capital expenditure — long-term investment in assets such as infrastructure.
  • Transfer payments — payments with no output in return, such as benefits and pensions (excluded from G in AD).

Taxes exist to fund this spending, manage AD, correct market failures and redistribute income.

front_old: Why is the classification of merit and demerit goods a value judgement, and how does imperfect information cause their mis-provision?
back_old:
The labels rest on a value judgement and can change over time — alcohol was once treated as a merit good; vaccinations were once distrusted.

Note too that not every good with consumption externalities is a merit or demerit good.

Imperfect information compounds the problem: consumers underestimate the long-term benefits of fruit and vegetables (under-consumption) and the health risks of smoking (over-consumption).
